Generating more learning cycles and limiting risk to a smaller time frame
Letting the team skip Sprint Planning when the backlog is already clear
explanation: Shorter Sprints can be employed to generate more learning cycles and limit the risk of cost and effort to a smaller time frame. All events still happen in every Sprint.

stem: Can items that do not meet the Definition of Done be presented at the Sprint Review?
options: Yes, if they are labelled as unfinished during the demo
Yes, if the Product Owner agrees that they are nearly done
Only if the stakeholders asked for those items specifically
No; work that is not Done is neither presented nor released
explanation: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review.

stem: Which artifact is the Product Owner accountable for managing?
options: The Product Backlog
The Increment
The burn-down chart
The Sprint Backlog
explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management. The Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers.

stem: What is lean thinking's main contribution to Scrum?
options: Adding review gates between project phases
Reducing waste and focusing on the essentials
Giving each task to the most efficient specialist
Fixing the scope early to protect the budget
explanation: Lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials. Fixed scope, phase gates and specialist hand-offs are not part of Scrum's foundation.

stem: A Developer asks the Scrum Master to update the Sprint Backlog for the team every morning. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Ask the Product Owner to take on updating the Sprint Backlog each morning
Agree, but only on days when the Developers are especially busy with work
Coach the Developers that the Sprint Backlog is their plan to keep up to date
Agree, since keeping the Sprint Backlog current is part of the Scrum Master's job
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers, and keeping it current is part of their self-management.

stem: True or false: The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.
options: True
False
explanation: The Scrum Guide says the entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.

stem: True or false: Each Sprint may be considered a short project.
options: True
False
explanation: The Scrum Guide says each Sprint may be considered a short project.

stem: True or false: A burn-down chart is a required Scrum artifact.
options: True
False
explanation: The three artifacts are the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment. Burn-downs are one of several optional ways to forecast progress.

stem: True or false: The Product Owner may reorder the Product Backlog at any time.
options: True
False
explanation: The Product Backlog is emergent, and ordering it is the Product Owner's accountability. Only changes to the current Sprint's scope are limited by the Sprint Goal.

stem: True or false: A team may change Scrum's rules and still call the result Scrum, as long as the Scrum Master agrees.
options: True
False
explanation: The Scrum framework as described in the Scrum Guide is immutable. A team can use extra practices inside it, but changing or dropping its rules means the result is not Scrum.

stem: True or false: The Scrum Master helps everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, both within the Scrum Team and in the organization.
options: True
False
explanation: The Scrum Guide says the Scrum Master does this by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, within the Scrum Team and the organization.

stem: What does the Scrum Guide say about the Developers' skills?
options: They must each hold a certificate in at least one technology
They must all be software programmers with the same training
They are often broad and vary with the domain of the work
They are narrow specialists who each own one product layer
explanation: The specific skills the Developers need are often broad and vary with the domain of work. Scrum is used well beyond software.

stem: What happens in Sprint Planning's 'how' topic?
options: The Scrum Master assigns the selected items to the Developers with the most suitable skills
The stakeholders approve the technical design before the Developers start any of the work
The Product Owner writes the detailed tasks so that the Developers know exactly what to do
The Developers plan the work needed to create an Increment that meets the Definition of Done
explanation: For each selected item, the Developers plan the work necessary to create an Increment that meets the Definition of Done, often by decomposing it into smaller work items. How this is done is at their sole discretion.

stem: How does the Product Goal relate to the Product Backlog?
options: It is in the Product Backlog, and the rest of it emerges to define what will fulfill the goal
It sits outside the Product Backlog in a separate charter that only the sponsor may change
It is the top item of the Product Backlog and is completed in the very next Sprint
It replaces the Product Backlog once the Scrum Team has been working for a few Sprints
explanation: The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define what will fulfill the Product Goal.

stem: How should the Product Owner treat feedback from the Sprint Review?
options: As a list of changes the team must make now
As a score for the Developers' performance
As input that may change the Product Backlog
As a formal approval of the Sprint's results
explanation: Feedback at the Sprint Review is input for adapting the Product Backlog. The Product Owner decides how it affects the order.

stem: Which value helps Scrum Team members do the right thing and work on tough problems even when it is uncomfortable?
options: Commitment
Openness
Courage
Respect
explanation: The Scrum Guide describes courage as having the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems.

stem: When does the Scrum Master facilitate stakeholder collaboration?
options: As requested or needed
Only during the Sprint Review
Only with written approval
Instead of the Product Owner
explanation: The Scrum Guide says the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner by facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed.

stem: Stakeholders keep emailing Developers directly with new requests. What should the Developers do?
options: Ask the Scrum Master to decide which of the requests deserve to be worked on
Work on the quickest requests first to keep the stakeholders happy and engaged
Point the stakeholders to the Product Owner, who manages the Product Backlog
Add the requests to the Sprint Backlog so nothing gets lost during the Sprint
explanation: New work goes through the Product Owner, who decides whether and where it belongs in the Product Backlog. Adding requests directly to the Sprint bypasses the Product Owner and can endanger the Sprint Goal.

stem: The Sprint Retrospective keeps running well over its timebox. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Let it run as long as it needs, since improvement matters more than any timebox in Scrum
Replace it with a survey that the Developers fill in on their own after each Sprint
Hold it only every other Sprint so that the team has more time for each one of them
Help the team keep within the timebox, for example by focusing on the most helpful changes
explanation: The Scrum Master ensures that all Scrum events take place and are positive, productive and kept within the timebox. Focusing on the most helpful changes is one way to do that.

stem: Which statement about the Sprint Backlog is correct?
options: It is owned by the Product Owner, who updates it after each Daily Scrum
It is a fixed list that cannot change once Sprint Planning has been completed
It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work the Developers plan to do
It is hidden from the stakeholders so that they do not interfere with the work
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers: a highly visible, real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.

stem: Which two are part of the Product Owner's accountability? (Choose two.)
options: Facilitating the Daily Scrum
Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items
Ordering Product Backlog items
Deciding how many hours each task takes
Removing the Developers' impediments
explanation: Creating, communicating and ordering Product Backlog items are part of the Product Owner's accountability. Sizing belongs to the Developers, and causing impediments to be removed to the Scrum Master.

stem: Why does Scrum rely on short, repeated cycles in a complex environment?
options: Short cycles let the team avoid planning and simply work on whatever arrives first
Short cycles make the full scope and date fixed and certain from day one
Each cycle is a phase gate where managers approve or stop the next one
Each cycle produces something to inspect, so the team learns and adapts early
explanation: In complex work what will happen is unknown, so Scrum uses short cycles that each produce a result to inspect. That feedback lets the team adapt early instead of following a prediction.

stem: The Product Owner uses the Daily Scrum to hand out new tasks to Developers. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Coach the Product Owner and Developers that the Developers plan their own work
Run the Daily Scrum personally so that all the tasks are shared out fairly among them
Let it continue, since the Product Owner knows which work matters most
Ask the Product Owner to send the tasks by email before the Daily Scrum
explanation: The Daily Scrum is the Developers' event, and they decide how to do the work. The Product Owner influences what is built through the Product Backlog, not by assigning tasks.

stem: Which three are accountabilities within a Scrum Team? (Choose three.)
options: Developers
Project Manager
Scrum Master
Team Lead
Product Owner
explanation: The Scrum Guide defines three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers. There is no project manager or team lead accountability in Scrum.

stem: Which two of these are Scrum events? (Choose two.)
options: Release planning
Sprint Review
Sprint Zero
Sprint Planning
Product Backlog refinement
explanation: The Scrum events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective. Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, and release planning and Sprint Zero are not in the Scrum Guide.

stem: Which two of these are commitments in Scrum? (Choose two.)
options: Definition of Ready
Velocity
Sprint forecast
Definition of Done
Product Goal
explanation: The three commitments are the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done. Velocity, forecasts and a Definition of Ready are not Scrum commitments.

stem: A stakeholder asks the Product Owner for a fixed, detailed plan for the next 12 months. What is the best response?
options: Decline to plan past the current Sprint, since Scrum does not allow longer-term planning
Produce a detailed task plan for all 12 months and hold the whole team to it without any changes
Share the Product Goal and a forecast, and explain that the plan will adapt as the team learns
Ask the Scrum Master to write the 12-month plan, since planning is part of their role
explanation: Scrum supports longer-term direction through the Product Goal and forecasts based on real progress, while keeping the plan open to adaptation as more is learned.

stem: Which two of these are Scrum Values? (Choose two.)
options: Simplicity
Transparency
Respect
Inspection
Focus
explanation: The five Scrum Values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. Transparency and inspection are empirical pillars, and simplicity is not one of the Scrum Values.

stem: Which two of these are impediments a Scrum Master might help remove? (Choose two.)
options: A shared test environment that is often unavailable
Slow decisions from a department outside the team
The Product Owner ordering the backlog
The Sprint Retrospective
The Definition of Done
explanation: Impediments are things that block the team's progress, such as unavailable environments or slow outside decisions. Scrum events, the Definition of Done and the Product Owner's accountability are part of the framework, not impediments.

stem: What should a Scrum Team's size allow it to do?
options: Remain nimble yet complete significant work in a Sprint
Give every single stakeholder a representative on the team
Cover every possible skill with a dedicated specialist
Run two Sprints in parallel when deadlines are tight
explanation: The Scrum Team should be small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically 10 or fewer people.

stem: Can Product Backlog refinement happen during a Sprint?
options: No; refinement happens only in a special Sprint before development
Yes; refinement is ongoing, and the backlog is refined as needed
Only during Sprint Planning, when the Product Owner is present
Only in the Sprint Review, when stakeholders can give approval
explanation: During the Sprint, the Product Backlog is refined as needed. Refinement is an ongoing activity to add detail, such as description, order and size.

stem: Why must each Increment be thoroughly verified?
options: So that the Scrum Master can sign each Increment off
So that the Sprint Review can act as a release gate
So that testing can be skipped in the following Sprints
So that all Increments work together and the result is usable
explanation: Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. To provide value, the Increment must be usable.

stem: In Scrum, value is delivered mainly through:
options: Usable Increments that meet the Definition of Done
Detailed documents that are reviewed at phase gates
Status reports that are sent to stakeholders weekly
Tasks that each Developer completes on their own
explanation: Value comes from usable Increments that meet the Definition of Done. Documents and reports may support the work but are not the product.

stem: Which is the best description of Scrum?
options: A project management process for planning a fixed scope against a fixed date and budget
A set of software engineering practices for writing and testing code faster than before
A detailed methodology that prescribes every single practice a team needs to deliver a product
A lightweight framework for generating value through adaptive solutions to complex problems
explanation: The Scrum Guide defines Scrum as a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. It is not limited to software and does not prescribe every practice.

stem: The team lacks a skill it needs for upcoming work. What fits Scrum best?
options: The Product Owner removes every item that needs the skill from the Product Backlog
The team works out how to gain or obtain the skill, since it is cross-functional as a whole
The Scrum Master hires a specialist for the team and assigns all of the related tasks to them
The work is handed to another department, and the team waits for it to be returned
explanation: A Scrum Team is cross-functional, with all the skills needed to create value each Sprint. A self-managing team decides how to close a skill gap, coached by the Scrum Master.

stem: Which statement about Developers is correct?
options: They must each specialize in a single layer of the product and stay in that layer
They report to the Scrum Master, who decides which of the tasks each of them works on
They are only the programmers; testers and designers sit outside the Scrum Team
They are the people committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint
explanation: Developers are the people in the Scrum Team committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint, whatever their specialty.

stem: According to the Scrum Guide, why is the Daily Scrum held at the same time and place every working day?
options: To meet a compliance requirement
To let managers attend it easily
To let stakeholders plan their day
To reduce complexity
explanation: The Scrum Guide says the Daily Scrum is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint to reduce complexity.

stem: There is no organizational standard. The Developers want to add 'performance tested' to their Definition of Done. Who decides?
options: The Product Owner alone, since quality affects the value
Management, since the change affects all the release dates
The Scrum Team, since it creates its own Definition of Done
The Scrum Master, since the Scrum Master owns the process
explanation: When the Definition of Done is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team creates one appropriate for the product, and it can strengthen it, for example after a Retrospective.

stem: The Developers often build items that turn out to be misunderstood. Which practice helps most?
options: Refining items together so the Developers understand them before Sprint Planning
Asking the Scrum Master to check each item after it is built and before review
Having the Product Owner write longer specifications and stop answering questions
Letting stakeholders test each item in production and report the problems found
explanation: Product Backlog refinement adds detail and shared understanding so items can be Done within a Sprint. The Product Owner and Developers work on it together as an ongoing activity.
